candidates.title: Dead Reckoning
candidates.pitch: A storm has killed every screen on the boat, so the instructor turns it into a drill: you get a periscope, a stopwatch and a grease pencil. You raise the scope for a few seconds, swing it onto an unmanned target barge, turn the handwheel until the two images of its mast meet to read the range, then drop below and pencil the fix on the chart. Two fixes reveal the barge's course and speed, you slide the aim point along its track until the practice round and the barge arrive together, and a dye splash tells you how good you were.
candidates.whyNow: Jam season: two outlets report Ludum Dare winding down toward 2028, and Ludum Dare 60 is listed for 16-19 October (as of 2026-10-11, per its page). One weekend jam page also reportedly lists 'Systems Offline' as its theme (single source, unconfirmed). This is the analog answer to that prompt: when the systems go dark, do it by hand.

research.summary: Hook, honestly rated: the Patch Notes jam page on itch.io lists 'Systems Offline' for a 72-hour jam on 9-12 October 2026, but the same page also says theme TBA and a search of the host's own newsletter found only earlier editions, so the page shows the theme as reported, not confirmed. What is verified shapes the mechanic: a periscope stadimeter converts the angle a mast subtends into range once the mast height is known, using two images offset by a handwheel, and accuracy depends on knowing the height, so the game needs a recognition book and several looks. Bearings alone from a stationary observer give no unique track, so the final drill removes the stadimeter and makes the player move the boat to build a baseline. Dead reckoning projects a fix forward from speed, heading and time, which is what the aim point does. Ludum Dare 60 is listed for 16-19 October and two outlets report the series ending in 2028.

facts.claim: A periscope stadimeter turns the angle a target's mast subtends into range once the mast height is known: two images offset by a handwheel or knob are lined up so the masthead meets the waterline, and range is read against the height entered. A wrong height means a wrong range.
From bearings alone, a single stationary observer cannot determine a unique target track; the observer has to maneuver for range to become observable.
Dead reckoning estimates a current position from a previously determined position plus speed, heading and elapsed time; the result is an estimate, not a fix.
As of 2026-10-11 two outlets report that the long-running Ludum Dare game jam is winding down and will end in 2028.
Ludum Dare 60 is listed for 16-19 October 2026 on its official page (single source, as of 2026-10-11, per ldj.am).
As of 2026-10-11, one jam page (Patch Notes v2.0 on itch.io) is reported to list 'Systems Offline' as its theme for 9-12 October 2026; the page also carries a theme-TBA line, so this is unconfirmed.

inspirations: Grease-pencil plotting boards and paper chart tables

design.coreLoop: Each drill sends one to three unmanned barges across a range at constant course and speed. You raise the scope (a spray timer limits each look), find a barge in low power, switch to high power, name its class from the recognition book and turn the handwheel until the stacked images meet to read range. You lower the scope and the fix is pencilled on the chart with bearing and clock time. You wait, look again, and the two marks give a track with an uncertainty wedge. You drag the aim point along the track until the practice round and the barge arrive together, then fire; the dye splash scores the miss distance, with bonuses for fewer looks and less exposure. Every extra look is a value-of-information bet: minute two is learning the handwheel, minute ten is choosing the gap between looks.
sophisticationHooks: Real optics: a stacked-image handwheel (two copies of the target, offset until the mast tip meets the waterline) turns a known mast height into range. The player's alignment error and a mis-identified ship class both skew the fix, and low power finds targets while high power measures.

Estimation with honesty: two timed fixes give a velocity vector drawn with an uncertainty wedge that narrows as the gap between looks grows, so waiting longer buys accuracy at the price of a barge that may sail out of range.

Equal-arrival aiming: dragging the aim point along the predicted track races two phosphor timing bars (practice round against barge) and a lamp lights when they match. A final drill takes the stadimeter away so the player must move the boat to build a baseline, as bearings-only tracking requires.

Hero moment: the scope broaches and a brass-ringed lens rises through the waterline, spray beading and clearing, horizon swaying with the swell; when the dye lands it blooms across the hull while the green readout answers with a soft afterglow. Reduced motion swaps the sway and spray for fades.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: seeded sim core (kinematics, reading-error model, scoring), periscope canvas with low and high power and four invented ship silhouettes, recognition book, stacked-image handwheel, SVG chart table with pencil fixes and uncertainty wedge, equal-arrival aiming with two timing bars, six drills ending in a graduation certificate, URL-hash seeds, instructor lines, muted-by-default WebAudio, reduced-motion twin, keyboard and touch controls, about panel with sources. Cut first: the bearings-only final drill, then swell-hidden waterlines. Not built: night, weather, other weapons, leaderboards, any backend.
risks: Hook is single-sourced and inconsistent: the page will show 'Systems Offline' as reported on a jam page, as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io, and the Ludum Dare 60 dates as per its official page; the game works without either.
Onboarding: optical ranging is unfamiliar. Drill 0 teaches it hands-on with a stationary barge, a Navigator's Assist toggle overlays the geometry, and the handwheel has keyboard steps.
Military flavour: keep it an exercise with unmanned barges and dye-marked practice rounds, invented ship classes, no insignia, no real vessel names, no casualties.
Realism: the model is simplified and the page says it is a game, not seamanship; historic details in the making-of come only from sources marked verified.
Precision on small screens: big hit areas, step buttons and assist rounding stop pixel-hunting at 360px.
Scope: the bearings-only final drill is cut first if the morning runs short.

candidates.title: Breaking Changes
candidates.pitch: A plain grey brick-breaker ships as v0.1. Between waves the studio offers two release candidates written in marketing-speak, such as 'Improved ball responsiveness' or 'Ceiling deprecated to improve performance'. You decode the euphemism, pick one, and play the next wave under its real rules while a board of system lamps shows what just went offline. A codex records what each phrase actually meant, and by v1.0 your build is a loud, glorious, thoroughly broken thing you assembled yourself.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless premise, since everyone has met a vague update note, with a jam-weekend nod: one jam page reportedly lists 'Systems Offline' as its theme (as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io, unconfirmed), and each patch here switches a game system off or on.

research.summary: Hook, honestly rated: the Patch Notes jam page on itch.io lists 'Systems Offline' for a 72-hour jam on 9-12 October 2026, but the page also says theme TBA and the host's own newsletter only shows earlier editions, so the theme is shown as reported, not confirmed, and the game stands without it. What is verified shapes the design: the 2012 juice talk by Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho used a plain Breakout-style game to show how layers of feedback transform feel, which gives the greybox-to-gold arc and the juice ladder; two separate support forums carry user complaints about stock release-note wording, which anchors the euphemism grammar in something people recognise; a Mini Jam page reportedly rates a mandatory limitation rather than the theme, which this idea turns into a per-wave limitation delivered as a patch note. All studio names, patches and quotes in the game are invented.

inspirations: The 2012 juice talk and its greybox-to-gold demo
Live-service balance patches and their notes

design.coreLoop: Wave loop: you read two patch notes, pick one with 1 or 2 (or a tap), watch the system-lamp board change as its true effect applies, then play a 30 to 40 second brick-breaker wave under every rule accumulated so far. Clearing the wave or losing a ball ends the loop with a 'known issues' reveal that tells you what the euphemism really meant and files it in the codex. Notes follow a learnable grammar (improved means faster with a catch, rebalanced means nerfed, deprecated means removed with compensation, reimagined means shuffled), so minute two is decoding and minute ten is routing synergies, such as a sticky paddle with gravity, around your build's weak spots. Ten waves end in a v1.0 launch card; three rollbacks end the run early. The daily seed makes the offers identical for everyone.
sophisticationHooks: A decodable grammar: eight verbs (improved, rebalanced, streamlined, reimagined, modernized, deprecated, added in beta, fixed) act on eight game systems (ball, paddle, ceiling, bricks, gravity, input, audio, juice), so a euphemism means the same kind of change everywhere. A codex fills in as you learn, which is what separates minute two from minute ten.

Generic modifier engine with synergy and clamps: about 40 valid verb-noun pairs stack, such as a sticky paddle with gravity or multiball with the ceiling deprecated, while a stall watchdog ships an in-fiction hotfix if no brick falls for 25 seconds.

The juice ladder: feedback layers (hit-stop, squash and stretch, trails, particles, shake, synthesized sound) arrive as patches, so the page shows game feel being built from silent grey boxes at v0.1 to a bright, noisy v1.0. Each layer has a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle.

Hero moment: a board of system lamps clicks off or on when a patch lands, an installing-update wipe sweeps the playfield, and the same bricks that were flat grey rectangles burst into confetti by v1.0 while the changelog scrolls alongside.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: fixed-step brick-breaker with sub-stepped collisions, a verb-by-noun patch engine (8 verbs, 8 systems, about 40 valid pairs) with flavor text, two-card picker, system-lamp board, codex, juice ladder with reduced-motion twins, muted-by-default WebAudio blips, ten waves with rollbacks and a v1.0 launch card, URL-hash seed and share string, keyboard and touch controls, about panel with sources. Cut first: unlockable skins, boss wave, extra brick types. Not built: leaderboards, any backend.
risks: Hook is single-sourced and inconsistent: the page shows 'Systems Offline' as reported on a jam page, as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io (unconfirmed); the game does not depend on it.
Brick-breakers are crowded: distinctness rides on the decodable verb grammar, the codex and the writing, so the spec should protect those before extra polish.
Soft-locks and balance: clamp every parameter, ship an in-fiction hotfix that reverts the last patch if no brick falls for 25 seconds, and let the QA monkey test random builds.
Humor stays generic: invented studio, patches and quotes; aim at the genre of vague release notes, never at a real company or product, and list the forum threads only as sources.
Motion and flashing: cap flashes below 3 per second, give every shake or flash a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle, start audio muted.
Scope: a generic verb-by-noun engine avoids hand-coding dozens of patches; skins, boss waves and extra brick types are cut first.
